Absolutely crazy to call this 2,000 word piece“CONTENT”!! And I really doubt you’d would not have this super angry tone to my face, you’d explain to me why you disagree with it, which is fine! But this assumption of bad intent is really uncalled for.
If you are only looking at it through the lens of US law then yes, that’s correct. It’s possible to have a broader conversation about it as well.

For the record, none of this my “preferred answer.” I had questions and asked some people. This article is what they said. Y’all are really pushing the assumption of bad intent on me and I doubt you’d do this to my face. Like, if you disagree, cool! Have a convo. Damn.
This is very helpful for my understanding, thank you for the thread

So even if there's an assumption that the goods are associated with Pattie Gonia, there's also a good chance that there's a simultaneous association of the same goods with Patagonia. That carries brand risk - it's unlikely to cost them the mark, but it does have real risk of weakening the mark.

The commercial rights that Pattie is seeking fall squarely within Patagonia's areas of actual use. I think it is very reasonable, in this media and commercial environment, for consumers to expect that "Pattie Gonia Hiking Club" sweatshirts (a real product) are done as an official colab.

But as a practitioner, it would be borderline malpractice (I'm not sure what side of the border) to recommend not taking action under these specific circumstances. It's not just a drag performer's artistic use; it's the drag performer's commercial entity seeking exclusive rights to commercial use.

That's bad. The more of the commons that's converted to private ownership, the less there is for everyone else - including artists and the public at large. That's bad. (Worth note here, though: Pattie was asking to fence some of the commons for herself; the public loses the ground either way.)

On the duty to police, there are extremely few examples of actual loss of a mark through failure to police, and I can think of none at all where a single lapse was sufficient to cause loss of the mark. And vigorous policing means taking an expansive view of ownership - it fences more of the commons.

Two things that are simultaneously true: 

1: I agree with @lexlanham.bsky.social (quoted in the article): duty to police is overblown, and in ways that are damaging to art and the public.

2: As a practitioner, I would be unable to recommend that Patagonia refrain from action here.

This is very good.

There are multiple levels to this case, within the IP case, as well as outside of it.

Have seen people saying to the company: "You can't trademark the name of a region" (actually, you can for different purposes).

But there are broader issues all together (for many big orgs)

Re: Patagonia v. Pattie Gonia 

I spoke with a trademark attorney and two scholars of Indigenous Patagonian history to understand both the legal and ethical question everyone is asking.

The answers are way more complex than social media is making them out to be.
Sure, that doesn’t mean it’s not a valuable thing to think about

"“No company or individual could ever ethically claim exclusive commercial rights over a regional name like Patagonia,” Briones told me. “Capitalism or capitalist interests can neither transform everything into merchandise nor swallow up and benefit from everything in its own exclusive benefit.”"
Can Patagonia™ own Patagonia?
Why Kate Marvel left NASA. The prominent climate scientist explains how pronouns have become more important than the planet at the nation's space agency.
Why Shein bought Everlane. On this week’s podcast episode, Tracy and I go deep about fashion industry greenwashing.
Everlane was never eco-friendly. Everlane helped sell the idea that buying lots of new clothes could be good for the climate. Now that marketing belongs to Shein.
Hantavirus is a climate story. Scientists tell HEATED the hantavirus outbreak is a warning that climate change is scrambling the boundaries between humans, wildlife, and disease.

Trump’s NOAA cuts would save less than a day and a half of Iran War spending. There's always money for war. But when it comes to protecting people from climate disasters, suddenly we're told the cupboard is bare.
UPDATE: Trump’s DOJ swoops in to save Big Oil. Trump’s DOJ just sued Minnesota to stop its climate deception case, right as it was finally allowed to move toward discovery.
Plastic detox update #1. I expected there’d be a high financial cost to avoiding plastic. I didn’t realize there’d be a social cost, too.
Republicans introduce extreme bill to ban lawsuits against Big Oil forever. Shouldn't Democrats... be saying something about this?
Detoxing my life, resentfully. Some thoughts on plastic, power, and personal responsibility.
What should we ask the plastic doctor?
Chevron's CEO made $104 million while America bombed Iran. America's oil executives have pocketed $1.4 billion selling stock during the Iran war, a new investigation shows.
Oil worker says fracking waste eroded his jaw. An elementary school was built atop the site where the radioactive waste was spread, journalist Saul Elbein reports.

Why smart people believe myths about electric cars (by Tracy Wholf). EVs should be having their moment, but misinformation is standing in the way. We spoke to a researcher about how to course correct.
